chunks: Redundancy in system design. The question: What is redundancy in a system? When is it preferred? How can you design a system with redundancy?
Redundancy means having more than one way to do an important job, so that one failure does not stop the whole system.
It is worth paying for when a failure is dangerous, when you cannot reach the system to repair it, or when downtime is very costly.
It is not free, so cheap everyday products usually skip it.
A spare tire is redundancy for a flat. It only helps if you notice the flat, and if you have the tools to swap it.
It would not help if a single nail strip flattened all four tires at once.
The lesson: a spare needs a way to detect the failure, a way to switch over, and a different weak point from the original.

the parallel pair is always above a single unit; TMR is better early but crosses below a single unit at t equals log 2 over about 69 300 h, because once the units are likely to have failed, needing two of three working is harder than needing one of one.
TMR is for missions much shorter than the MTBF. Drag λ up to 0. 03 per 1,000 h: every curve falls sooner, and the TMR crossover moves in to about 23,100 h.
Single point of failure: one part whose failure alone stops the whole system. Failover: switching from the failed unit to the spare.
Common-cause failure: one problem, such as a shared power supply, that knocks out every copy at once.
Voting: with three copies, taking the answer that at least two agree on, so one wrong copy is outvoted.
Reliability: the probability that a unit still works at the end of a given time.
Suppose one power supply has a 99% chance of surviving a 1000-hour mission. That means a 1% chance it fails. Add a second, identical supply so that either one can run the load.
Now the load only goes dark if both fail. If they fail independently, that chance is 0. 01 times 0. 01 equals 0. 0001 . Reliability rises from 99% to 99. 99%.
That only works if three things hold. The system must notice the failure, the switch itself must not fail, and both supplies must not die from a shared cause.
That is the whole idea.
"Redundancy means having more than one way to do a critical function so a single failure doesn't stop the system.
I'd use it when failure is dangerous, expensive or can't be repaired, like aircraft, cars, medical devices and satellites.
You can run parallel units, keep a standby, or use three-way voting.
The catches are that you must detect failures, the switch can itself fail, and common-cause faults like a shared supply bypass it.
It costs power, size and money, so I only use it where the risk justifies it."
